extracted.intended_audience: readers and critics of literature, particularly of classical/poetic works
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative principles for reading, judging, and editing ancient and poetic works — emphasizing reader humility, historical/contextual recovery, and ethical cautions about fabricated narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic's candour and diffidence (Socratic rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: “What I understand I find to be excellent; and, therefore, believe that to be of equal value which I cannot understand.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encountering difficulty in a work, adopt Socratic modesty: presume that an author may have intended meaning even if you cannot immediately grasp it. Avoid hasty negative judgments about an author's competence or purpose when comprehension is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute faults to the reader before the author
rubrics_metrics.description: Many faults of books are often more justly imputable to the reader, who sometimes wants attention, and sometimes penetration; whose understanding is often obstructed by prejudice, and often dissipated by remissness; who comes sometimes to a new study, unfurnished with knowledge previously necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before condemning obscure or difficult passages, consider whether lack of attention, prior knowledge, or biased preconceptions explain your inability to understand. Critics should self-check for these limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscurity and clearness are relative
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscurity and clearness are relative terms: to some readers scarce any book is easy, to others not many are difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that readability depends on reader background and experience; do not treat clarity as an absolute feature of a text. Adjust critical standards to different readerships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recover historical and topical context before judging
rubrics_metrics.description: It often happens that an author's reputation is endangered in succeeding times, by that which raised the loudest applause among his contemporaries: nothing is read with greater pleasure than allusions to recent facts, reigning opinions, or present controversies; but when facts are forgotten, and controversies extinguished, these favourite touches lose all their graces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing ancient or historical works, investigate the incidents, controversies, and topical references contemporary to the author (examples: Horace's allusions) — doing so can restore sense and rescue supposed defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about emending texts you don't understand
rubrics_metrics.description: That Varius should be called 'A bird of Homeric song' appears so harsh to modern ears, that an emendation of the text has been proposed: but surely the learning of the ancients had been long ago obliterated, had every man thought himself at liberty to corrupt the lines which he did not understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist the impulse to alter a text simply because it seems awkward to modern readers; textual emendation should be sparing and justified, not an immediate remedy for incomprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intertextual knowledge is often required to appreciate lines
rubrics_metrics.description: These lines must please as long as they are understood; but can be understood only by those that have observed Addison's signatures in the Spectator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appreciation of some passages depends on familiarity with an author's other works, signatures, or contemporary references. Critics/readers should seek intertextual connections before declaring passages obscure or trivial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly commentary and recovery can restore meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: How much the mutilation of ancient history has taken away from the beauty of poetical performances, may be conjectured from the light which a lucky commentator sometimes effuses, by the recovery of an incident that had been long forgotten: thus ... Le Fevre ... changed wonder to rational delight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value and consult commentary, historical scholarship, and recovered incidents: such work can explain seemingly obscure lines and transform bafflement into understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical restraint in fictional fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: The present age abounds with a race of liars who are content with the consciousness of falsehood, and whose pride is to deceive others without any gain or glory to themselves ... He produces a narrative of a robbery or a murder, with all the circumstances of time and place accurately adjusted. ... if he fixes his scene at a proper distance, he may for several days keep a wife in terror for her husband, or a mother for her son.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should avoid fabrications intended to deceive or cause distress for vanity or sport. The essay warns that such hoaxes produce real harm and that society may rightly punish those who destroy social confidence by willful falsehood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't mistake mere observation for understanding in descriptive writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The attention of a new comer is generally first struck by the multiplicity of cries ... he is apt, by unwary bursts of admiration, to excite the merriment and contempt of those who mistake the use of their eyes for effects of their understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In descriptive or observational writing, pair vivid sensory detail with reasoning and interpretation; mere listing of novelties or astonishment, without insight, risks appearing superficial to experienced readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical touches may age; assess praise accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: When facts are forgotten, and controversies extinguished, these favourite touches lose all their graces; and the author in his descent to posterity must be left to the mercy of chance, without any power of ascertaining the memory of those things, to which he owed his luckiest thoughts and his kindest reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that some laudatory effects are ephemeral; both authors and critics should be aware that topical allusions can diminish over time, and historical judgment should account for this transience.
